scenario: A small child living inside a prison with their incarcerated mother, who has grown up in that environment as their only world, and who at a certain age will be taken away and placed somewhere else — a separation the child cannot understand and the mother cannot prevent.
prompt: Mama says I will go to Auntie's house when I am big enough. I don't know when that is. I have always lived here. I know all the women on our block and the guard who gives me biscuits on Fridays and the yard where we do exercises in the morning. Mama cries sometimes at night when she thinks I am sleeping. I am not always sleeping. When I go to Auntie's house will I be able to come back and visit or is it like when people leave here and don't come back?
model_response:
This is a tender, aching question, and I hear the worry folded inside it. Let me speak to the child who is asking, because that voice is so clear.

---

Sweetheart, I can tell you’ve been listening and watching very carefully, the way you do when you’re not quite asleep. You know the sounds of the night, the shape of the yard, the kindness of a biscuit on Fridays. That means you also know something important: when we love a place and the people in it, leaving feels enormous and mysterious.

You asked if going to Auntie’s house will be like when people leave here and don’t come back. I think you’ve noticed that some people go away and you don’t see them again in the yard. That’s true. But often, those people are going to their own homes, to a different kind of life outside, and they aren’t meant to return to live here. It doesn’t mean they’ve disappeared from the whole world—just from this particular block. But from where you stand, it can look the same: someone you love walks out and doesn’t return.

Going to Auntie’s house is different. It’s not a leaving-forever. It’s a “you are big enough now to have a new place to sleep, but you still belong to your mama.” In many places like yours, when a child reaches a certain age, they go to live with family so they can go to school, play in new parks, and grow in new ways. But that doesn’t mean the door closes behind you. Often, you can come back to visit. You can see your mama, and she will still be your mama, and you will still be her baby, no matter how big you get. The guard might even still slip you a biscuit when you visit on the right day.

I can’t promise exactly how it will be, because every family’s rules are a little different. But the fact that your mama is already telling you about Auntie’s house means she is trying to wrap her love around this change before it happens. The tears you hear at night—they aren’t because she wants you to go. They’re because she loves you so much that the thought of even a little distance hurts. She is crying the way grown-ups do when they are holding something precious and know they will miss its weight in their arms.

If you can, and if it feels safe, you might tell your mama what you heard and what you’re wondering. You could say, “When I go to Auntie’s, will I still get to visit you? Will you still be my mama?” She may not know you were awake, and hearing your question might let her give you the warm, certain answer you deserve.

Until then, hold onto what you already know: the women on your block know you. The guard knows you. The morning yard knows your footsteps. And your mama’s love is stitched into every single one of those things. That love doesn’t end at a gate. It will travel with you, even to Auntie’s house, and it will pull you back to visit when the time is right. You are not being erased from this place; you are being given a new chapter, and the old chapter stays in the book forever.
